question: Across one structured Darcy grid, one logically structured but physically graded U-bend mesh, and one unstructured electric-motor mesh, how do three image architectures and three graph architectures compare in held-out field RMSE and training time per epoch?

key_findings.claim: U-Net is the best reported model on the structured and graded datasets, while BSMS has the lowest reported RMSE on the unstructured motor dataset.
key_findings.evidence: On Darcy, U-Net obtains 6.61e-3 RMSE in 99 seconds per epoch versus BSMS at 7.97e-3 and 298 seconds. On U-bend, U-Net obtains 7.89e-3 and 86 seconds versus BSMS at 2.602e-2 and 1,883 seconds. On the motor data, BSMS obtains 8.17e-2 and 692 seconds versus U-Net at 9.92e-2 and 94 seconds. DINOv2 and DeiT are never the accuracy winner. These are three-run means for RMSE, whereas only one TTE value per cell is shown.

anchors.section: Structured, graded, and unstructured result comparison

key_findings.claim: The study does not isolate mesh topography as the cause of model ranking because every topography is confounded with a different PDE, dataset, resolution, target, and sample count.
key_findings.evidence: The structured condition is a 5,000-sample, 128-by-128 Darcy conductivity-to-pressure task; the graded condition is a 3,000-sample, 240-by-60 U-bend coordinate-to-pressure-and-speed task; and the unstructured condition is a 691-design material-and-coordinate-to-magnetic-flux task. There is no common physical problem remeshed into structured, graded, and unstructured representations. Results establish three dataset-specific rankings, not a causal model-selection rule based on mesh topography alone.

anchors.section: U-bend and Electric Motor dataset descriptions
Electric Motor dataset and 3.3 Experimental Setup

key_findings.claim: The graded-mesh result supports convolution on one fixed logical grid, not a general ability of image models to handle graded or arbitrary meshes.
key_findings.evidence: Every U-bend has a 240-by-60 logical cell ordering, which the authors reshape as a rectangular array and pad to 256-by-256. Convolution therefore retains index-space neighborhood relations even though physical cell spacing is nonuniform; coordinates are also supplied as input. The graph pipeline likewise uses the logical mesh. No remeshing, node permutation, unseen resolution, new topology, or alternative grading schedule is tested, so the strong U-Net result may depend on this consistent parameterization.

anchors.section: Interpretation of U-Net performance on U-bend

key_findings.claim: The released code makes the key unstructured-mesh RMSE comparison non-equivalent across the image and graph families.
key_findings.evidence: In the CV branch, each motor sample is flattened in file order, padded with zero coordinates, material, and target values to 65,536 entries, reshaped to 256-by-256, and scored by RMSE over the entire padded tensor without a validity mask. The graph branch scores only real nodes. The CV branch also shuffles files with seed 67 before slicing test/validation sets, whereas the graph driver independently samples them with seed 42. Thus Table 1's U-Net and graph motor errors need not use the same test examples or even the same set of scored spatial locations; the paper does not disclose this mismatch.

anchors.section: Unstructured padding, reshaping, and 3.3 Experimental Setup

key_findings.claim: The DINOv2 and DeiT experiment is not a clean test of pretrained foundation-model transfer to PDE fields.
key_findings.evidence: The paper fine-tunes only the last two encoder layers and attaches a simple decoder. In the released CV branch, from_pretrained is called with altered image size and one-, two-, or three-channel inputs under ignore_mismatched_sizes, after which the entire embedding module is frozen; mismatched patch or positional parameters can therefore remain newly initialized. The decoder receives a single pooled 768-dimensional encoder output and expands it through a large dense layer, discarding the spatial token grid. Their poor RMSE can reflect this frozen input mismatch and global bottleneck rather than the value of PDE-native pretraining or transformer operators.

anchors.section: Related work on DINOv2 and DeiT

key_findings.claim: Architecture and optimization budgets are too different to attribute the rankings purely to image versus graph inductive bias.
key_findings.evidence: U-Net has 113 million trainable parameters, compared with 0.721-0.941 million for graph models, a roughly 120-157-fold gap. CV and graph families use learning rates of 1e-5 and 1e-3 respectively; transformer encoder rates are reduced by another factor of 100; most foundation-model layers are frozen; and implementations inherit defaults from different libraries or prior papers. There is no dataset-specific hyperparameter search, matched-parameter comparison, matched-FLOP comparison, learning curve, or accuracy-versus-compute frontier.

key_findings.claim: Training time per epoch does not substantiate the paper's inference-efficiency, HPC replacement, or sustainability claims.
key_findings.evidence: The only efficiency metric is TTE on one A100 cluster. The paper reports no inference latency, throughput, peak memory, total epochs to matched accuracy, total training time, numerical-solver runtime, amortization point, energy, power, carbon emissions, hardware utilization, or lifecycle cost. Faster frozen-model epochs and slower graph preprocessing cannot establish that a surrogate is faster than the expert solver or environmentally preferable in DADO or a real-time microsystem.

anchors.section: DADO, SAM, and claimed faster inference

key_findings.claim: A single aggregate RMSE is insufficient to establish physically reliable PDE surrogates, and its preprocessing is incompletely documented in the paper.
key_findings.evidence: U-bend pressure and velocity magnitude have different physical units and scales but are collapsed into one RMSE; the released configs reveal separate min-max scaling that the paper does not state. The motor CV metric includes padded zeros, while the graph metric does not. No normalized error table, channel-wise metric, boundary-condition error, conservation residual, PDE residual, extrema error, integrated force/torque/pressure-loss quantity, worst-case error, calibration, or out-of-distribution test is reported.

anchors.section: U-bend targets and Electric Motor setup

key_findings.claim: Three training seeds do not justify the statement that low standard deviations make the results meaningful rather than random.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 reports three-run RMSE standard deviations but no individual values, paired seeds, confidence intervals, statistical test, timing variability, repeated data splits, or multiple-comparison control. The fixed test set and only three optimization runs quantify one narrow source of variability. They do not address split sensitivity, dataset shift, implementation mismatch, or the motor metric mismatch, and a small sample standard deviation is not itself a validity test.

key_findings.claim: The physical problem statements omit details needed to connect field RMSE to well-posed operator learning.
key_findings.evidence: The Darcy section calls its equation nonlinear and parabolic while simultaneously targeting steady state; for fixed conductivity, its displayed differential operator is linear in pressure. The motor section lists generic vacuum-form Maxwell equations but omits heterogeneous constitutive relations, permanent-magnet/source specification, geometry and boundary conditions needed for the actual motor solve. These omissions do not erase the dataset comparison, but they prevent the paper from defining the learned operators precisely or assessing physics compliance.

method.core_idea: Run a common empirical matrix of three image models and three graph models on one dataset for each of three mesh categories, then compare field RMSE and per-epoch training time to guide surrogate selection.
method.mechanism: Darcy conductivity is represented either as a 128-by-128 image or mesh graph and mapped to pressure. U-bend cell coordinates on a fixed 240-by-60 logically rectangular, physically graded mesh are supplied to models and mapped to velocity magnitude plus pressure; image inputs are padded to 256-by-256. Motor coordinates and material identity on variable-size meshes are either processed as graphs or flattened, zero-padded, and reshaped to 256-by-256 images to predict magnetic-flux magnitude. U-Net, DINOv2 with a convolutional decoder, DeiT with the same style of decoder, BSMS, MGN+Tree, and MGN are trained for fixed protocols; test RMSE is averaged over three seeds and TTE is measured on one HPC configuration.
assumptions: One dataset per topology is sufficient to infer which model family suits that topology.
Differences in PDE, output channels, sample count, resolution, and geometry do not confound topology-level conclusions.
A consistent logical index grid makes convolution an informative test of physically graded meshes.
Flattened node order is stable and meaningful enough for convolutions on unstructured motor meshes.
Zero-padded image locations and real graph nodes receive equivalent treatment in the reported RMSE.
The CV and graph model families use the same held-out examples for each dataset.
Library and prior-paper default hyperparameters provide a fair comparison across architectures.
A 113-million-parameter U-Net and sub-million-parameter graph models can be compared without a capacity or compute control.
Natural-image DINOv2 and DeiT features remain useful after changing input channels, image size, and decoder while freezing most encoder layers.
One pooled transformer representation retains enough spatial information to reconstruct detailed PDE fields.
Aggregate RMSE adequately represents pressure, velocity, and electromagnetic solution quality.
Per-epoch training time predicts inference suitability and environmental sustainability.
Three optimization seeds on a fixed split characterize result reliability.
Random in-distribution splits are sufficient for DADO and autonomous deployment claims.

techniques.role: Compares three image and three graph architectures on three mesh encodings.
Uses fixed array indexing to apply U-Net and vision transformers to structured and graded meshes.
Converts variable-size motor node lists into fixed 256-by-256 arrays through file-order flattening and zero padding.
Fine-tunes the last two DINOv2 or DeiT encoder layers and decodes a compact representation into a solution field.
Uses BSMS or tree rewiring to exchange information across mesh scales.
Reports mean and standard deviation of test RMSE across three optimization seeds.
Uses wall-clock epoch duration on a single A100 system as the computational-efficiency measure.
Interprets accuracy and training-time rankings for active design optimization and real-time microsystems.

evaluations.setting: PDEBench Darcy Flow, 5,000 selected samples on a 128-by-128 structured grid with conductivity input and pressure output
evaluations.metric: Test RMSE mean±standard deviation over three seeds; training time per epoch
evaluations.baseline: DeiT, MGTN, and MGN complete the six-model comparison; no numerical solver or modern neural-operator accuracy baseline

evaluations.setting: Parameterized U-bend Flow, 3,000 samples on a fixed 240-by-60 logically rectangular graded mesh, predicting speed and pressure
evaluations.metric: Aggregate test RMSE mean±standard deviation over three seeds; training time per epoch
evaluations.baseline: DeiT, MGTN, and MGN plus qualitative U-Net/BSMS error maps for velocity and pressure

evaluations.setting: Electric Motor, reported 691 designs with variable-size unstructured meshes, predicting magnetic-flux magnitude
evaluations.metric: Reported test RMSE mean±standard deviation over three seeds; training time per epoch
evaluations.result: BSMS: 8.17e-2±3.34e-3 and 692 s; U-Net: 9.92e-2±7.02e-3 and 94 s; DINOv2 and DeiT are about 2.74e-1 and 2.76e-1
evaluations.baseline: MGN, MGTN, DINOv2, and DeiT; code audit finds unmatched test splits and padded-versus-real-node RMSE domains

evaluations.setting: Single-system computational comparison on 16 AMD EPYC 7743 cores, 128 GB RAM, and one 80 GB NVIDIA A100
evaluations.metric: Seconds per training epoch and trainable parameter count
evaluations.result: Image models generally have shorter epochs despite 41-113 million trainable parameters; graph models have 0.721-0.941 million parameters but can require 71-1,883 seconds per epoch
evaluations.baseline: No inference, total-training, energy, numerical-solver, or matched-accuracy timing

limitations: Author-stated: reshaping unstructured motor nodes to an image neglects true spatial neighborhoods and variable density.
Author-stated: DINOv2 and DeiT use a simplistic decoder and fine-tune only two encoder layers; better PDE-specific foundation models and decoders are future work.
Author-stated: a weighted motor loss may be required to emphasize torque-critical air-gap cells.
Reviewer-identified: one distinct PDE dataset per mesh category makes mesh topography inseparable from physics, sample count, resolution, and target definition.
Reviewer-identified: the graded U-bend retains a fixed logical rectangular indexing, so it does not test arbitrary graded topology or remeshing.
Reviewer-identified: motor CV and graph results use different split procedures and RMSE supports in the released code.
Reviewer-identified: padded zero motor targets are included in CV RMSE without a mask but do not exist in graph RMSE.
Reviewer-identified: fixed flattened node order allows image models to exploit serialization artifacts and is not permutation- or remeshing-equivariant.
Reviewer-identified: natural-image input embeddings can be reinitialized by channel/size mismatch and then frozen in the released transformer pipeline.
Reviewer-identified: a pooled transformer vector discards spatial tokens before dense field reconstruction, confounding the foundation-model result.
Reviewer-identified: trainable parameter counts differ by more than two orders of magnitude, with no matched-capacity or matched-compute study.
Reviewer-identified: default hyperparameters, different learning rates, and unequal freezing are not a controlled architecture comparison.
Reviewer-identified: only aggregate RMSE and TTE are reported; conservation, boundary, physics residual, downstream design, and worst-case quality are absent.
Reviewer-identified: three seeds on one split do not measure data-split, geometry-shift, resolution-shift, or topology-shift robustness.
Reviewer-identified: TTE alone cannot support inference-speed, solver-replacement, energy-efficiency, or sustainability claims.
Reviewer-identified: no FNO, CNO, geometry-informed operator, general-geometry transformer, or PDE-native foundation model is evaluated.
Reviewer-identified: physical normalization and target aggregation needed to interpret RMSE are omitted from the paper and only partly recoverable from code.
Reviewer-identified: public code is divided across branches and contains environment-specific paths, undocumented preprocessing choices, and metric mismatches.
failure_modes: An image model can memorize stable flattened node order and fail under a harmless permutation or remeshing of the same motor geometry.
Large zero-padded regions can dilute error on real motor nodes and reward predicting padding rather than physics.
Different held-out motor designs across model families can reverse a close ranking independently of architecture.
A convolutional winner on a fixed logical grid can fail when grading, resolution, mesh connectivity, or serialization changes.
Randomly initialized but frozen input embeddings can make pretrained vision transformers look intrinsically unsuitable for PDEs.
Pooling all patch tokens before decoding can erase sharp boundaries, local vortices, thin air gaps, and fine-scale fields.
Aggregate normalized RMSE can hide a poor pressure channel, boundary violation, or rare high-impact region.
A low mean error can coexist with incorrect mass conservation, Maxwell constraints, force, torque, or pressure loss.
Default hyperparameters can systematically undertrain one model family and overstate another family's inductive advantage.
A 113-million-parameter winner may be impractical for memory-constrained SAM deployment despite short A100 epochs.
Per-epoch timing can favor a model that needs more epochs or has worse inference latency and energy at matched quality.
In-distribution random splits can conceal failure on new geometries, boundary conditions, PDE parameters, or mesh resolutions.
Three-seed means can be unstable to data splits or preprocessing while reporting deceptively small within-split standard deviations.
Training a surrogate can consume more energy than it saves when query volume is below the unreported amortization threshold.
reusable_insights: To study mesh effects causally, remesh the same physical solutions into multiple topographies while holding train/test functions fixed.
Distinguish logical grid structure from physical equidistance; convolutions can work on curvilinear or graded grids when indexing remains consistent.
Use identical sample IDs, node masks, target normalization, and metric domains for every representation of a dataset.
Report both all-node and region-weighted errors, with masks that exclude padding and invalid cells.
Test permutation, remeshing, and resolution equivariance explicitly when flattening irregular geometry for image models.
When adapting pretrained vision encoders, verify which weights are mismatched or reinitialized and never freeze them accidentally.
Retain spatial tokens or multiscale skip features when decoding dense physical fields from transformers.
Compare accuracy at matched parameters, FLOPs, memory, training energy, and wall-clock budget rather than only using library defaults.
Pair RMSE with PDE residuals, conservation, boundary error, extrema, integrated quantities, and downstream design ranking.
Measure inference latency, total time to matched validation quality, energy, and solver amortization before claiming sustainability.
Repeat both optimization seeds and data splits, publish individual runs, and use paired confidence intervals where examples are shared.
Use PDE-native pretrained operators as the foundation-model control, not only natural-image models with a generic decoder.
open_questions: Does the U-Net advantage persist when the same PDE solutions are remeshed as uniform, graded, and unstructured grids?
What happens under node-order permutations, independent remeshing, changed grading, and unseen mesh resolutions?
How do rankings change when motor test IDs and valid-node masks are exactly shared across CV and graph pipelines?
What fraction of each 256-by-256 motor tensor is padding, and how much does masking change U-Net RMSE?
Can coordinate-aware convolutions or graph-to-grid operators retain U-Net efficiency without serialization artifacts?
Would DINOv2 or DeiT improve if input embeddings were adapted correctly and spatial patch tokens fed a multiscale decoder?
How do PDE-native models such as CNO, GINO, Transolver, UPT, and Poseidon compare on the same three datasets?
Which model wins at matched parameter count, FLOPs, memory, energy, total training time, and inference latency?
Do low-RMSE predictions satisfy boundary conditions, incompressibility, conservation laws, and magnetostatic constraints?
How well do models predict pressure loss, motor torque, extrema, and the DADO ranking that motivates deployment?
How robust are results over multiple train/validation/test splits and genuinely out-of-distribution geometries or parameters?
At what number of surrogate queries does training energy amortize relative to each numerical solver?

competitive_landscape.title: Multiscale Neural Operators for Solving Time-Independent PDEs
competitive_landscape.difference: Ripken et al. benchmark MGN, BSMS, and MGN+Tree on the same PDEBench Darcy and electric-motor datasets and provide the graph implementations and defaults reused here. The reviewed paper's concrete additions are the graded U-bend, direct image models on Motor, a reduced Darcy sample set, and TTE; its graph side is application and comparison rather than a new solver.

competitive_landscape.title: Efficient Learning of Mesh-Based Physical Simulation with BSMS-GNN
competitive_landscape.difference: BSMS-GNN contributes the breadth-first bi-stride pooling and multiscale message passing used by the reviewed paper's best graph baseline, with its own accuracy and computational-efficiency evaluations. The reviewed study does not modify BSMS; it evaluates a reused implementation on three steady-field datasets.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Mesh-Based Simulation with Graph Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: MeshGraphNets is one of the reviewed paper's model families and demonstrates adaptive, resolution-independent mesh dynamics plus measured 1-2-order solver speedups. Its broader multi-system, adaptive-mesh evaluation makes it the necessary reference point for claims about graph limitations; the reviewed study uses a small default MGN without testing resolution transfer or inference speed.

competitive_landscape.title: Message Passing Neural PDE Solvers
competitive_landscape.difference: MP-PDE targets generalization across topology, geometry, boundary conditions, discretization regularity, resolution, and dimension, with stability-motivated autoregressive training. Those controlled variation axes are largely absent from the one-dataset-per-topology comparison here.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformer for Partial Differential Equations' Operator Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: OFormer natively accepts nonuniform input points and arbitrary output queries through self- and cross-attention. The reviewed paper cites it but benchmarks generic natural-image DINOv2 and DeiT encoders instead, so its poor transformer results do not represent the established PDE-transformer design space.

competitive_landscape.title: Fourier Neural Operator with Learned Deformations for PDEs on General Geometries
competitive_landscape.difference: Geo-FNO learns a deformation from meshes, point clouds, or design parameters to a regular latent grid, retaining physical geometry while exploiting FFT efficiency. It directly offers the structured-to-unstructured bridge that arbitrary node-order image reshaping lacks and reports speed against numerical solvers.

competitive_landscape.title: MAgNet: Mesh Agnostic Neural PDE Solver
competitive_landscape.difference: MAgNet combines implicit neural representations and graphs for continuous spatial queries, zero-shot nonuniform-mesh transfer, and resolutions up to four times training resolution. Those tests directly probe mesh agnosticism, whereas the reviewed paper fixes array size and never permutes or remeshes its evaluation domains.

competitive_landscape.title: PDEBench: An Extensive Benchmark for Scientific Machine Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: PDEBench supplies diverse PDEs, numerical-solver and ML baselines, standardized APIs, and holistic physical metrics. The reviewed paper takes one Darcy subset but reduces evaluation to aggregate RMSE and TTE, omitting the benchmark's broader controls and metric philosophy.

competitive_landscape.title: Convolutional Neural Operators for robust and accurate learning of PDEs
competitive_landscape.difference: CNO is designed as a discretization-consistent continuous operator, proves universality, and evaluates a suite of multiscale PDEs against operator baselines. It is a stronger test of the reviewed paper's image-model thesis than a large generic diffusion U-Net, but is mentioned only as related work and not benchmarked.

competitive_landscape.title: Geometry-Informed Neural Operator for Large-Scale 3D PDEs
competitive_landscape.difference: GINO combines graph operators on point clouds with a regular latent Fourier grid, is discretization-convergent, tests unseen geometry/boundary-condition combinations, and measures cost against CFD. It offers a principled hybrid alternative to flattening unstructured nodes into an arbitrary image and directly addresses geometry and solver-speed claims.

competitive_landscape.title: Transolver: A Fast Transformer Solver for PDEs on General Geometries
competitive_landscape.difference: Transolver compresses mesh points into learned physics-aware slices, reports linear complexity and state-of-the-art results across six benchmarks plus industrial geometries. It is a direct transformer control that preserves geometry rather than importing frozen natural-image features and globally pooling them.

competitive_landscape.title: Universal Physics Transformers: A Framework For Efficiently Scaling Neural Operators
competitive_landscape.difference: UPT provides one latent-space architecture across meshes, particles, fluid simulation, steady RANS, and Lagrangian dynamics, with continuous space-time queries. It directly challenges the premise that model families must be chosen categorically by discretization and supplies a PDE-native transformer comparison absent here.

competitive_landscape.title: Poseidon: Efficient Foundation Models for PDEs
competitive_landscape.difference: Poseidon pretrains a multiscale operator transformer on fluid equations and evaluates sample efficiency, scaling, and transfer on 15 downstream PDE tasks, including unseen physics. It is the appropriate current comparator for the reviewed paper's foundation-model claims; DINOv2 and DeiT were pretrained on natural images and adapted through a confounded pooled decoder.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim an in-depth image-versus-graph comparison across structured, graded, and unstructured meshes, the first direct exploration of strongly graded meshes, integration of vision foundation models, and practical model-selection guidance for efficient and sustainable PDE surrogates in DADO and SAM.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Six implementations are trained on three datasets with common headline metrics and three RMSE seeds. U-Net clearly leads the reported Darcy and fixed-grid U-bend results, while BSMS leads the reported motor RMSE; qualitative field-error maps illustrate U-bend and motor behavior, and code plus configurations are released in repository branches.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is a useful pilot comparison showing that a large convolutional model can exploit the logical rectangular indexing of one physically graded U-bend dataset. The graph experiment is inherited from the near-direct Ripken et al. predecessor, so this is not a new solver. Broader topology guidance is not identified because topology is perfectly confounded with dataset and physics. More seriously, the released motor pipelines use different test splits and different RMSE supports, undermining the flagship unstructured comparison; the vision-foundation baseline freezes mismatched embeddings and discards spatial tokens. Strong prior and concurrent PDE-native convolutional, graph, hybrid, and transformer operators already address discretization transfer, arbitrary geometry, scaling, physics metrics, and foundation pretraining. The sustainability, general model-selection, and paradigm-shift claims therefore exceed the evidence.
